summary: A 1969 description of how to implement the host-to-host procedures in GORDO, a host system. It covers connections and links, message structure and user transactions, and then how to realise them in that system. It was replaced by RFC 33.

plainLanguage.summary: This note explains how one particular computer would follow the rules for talking to other computers. A newer note replaced it.

subtitle: Host-to-host communication implementation for the GORDO operating system

tldr.problem: In 1969, ARPANET research required working implementations of host-to-host protocols for actual computer systems, not just abstract specifications. GORDO, the UCLA host operating system, needed concrete software procedures and data structures to enable networking.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 11 specifies how GORDO implements connections (full-duplex bidirectional links between users at different hosts) using allocation tables to track outgoing links and connections, shared memory pages for user-network communication, and two main programs: the Handler (I/O interrupt routine) and the Network program (which manages connections and message formatting).
tldr.outcome: This was one of the earliest documented implementations of a host-to-host protocol in a real operating system, demonstrating how abstract networking concepts could be realized through careful management of memory, interrupts, and process coordination.

today: RFC 11 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 33. It represents one of the earliest documented implementations of network protocols in an actual operating system, providing valuable insight into how abstract networking concepts were realized in practice.

sections.title: Overview of Host-to-Host Procedures
sections.content: RFC 11 describes how GORDO, the UCLA host operating system running on an SDS Sigma 7, implements the host-to-host procedures defined in BBN reports 1822 and 1763. These procedures allow multiple user programs on one host to simultaneously use the network by sharing network resources. Each host needs a special Network program that multiplexes outgoing messages from users into the network and distributes incoming messages to the appropriate users. Connections are full-duplex (bidirectional) and defined between users at remote hosts, while links are the underlying directional communication paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Multiple users on one computer need to share access to the network. The operating system has a special program that sends everyone's messages out and brings everyone's replies back.

sections.title: Data Structures and Memory Management
sections.content: GORDO uses three allocation tables to manage connections and links. The HOST table (bit map, disc resident, indexed by remote host number) tracks free outgoing links, with a maximum of 64 links active at once across all remote hosts. The CONNECT table (disc resident, indexed by connection number) stores information about each connection including the user identification and the outgoing and incoming link numbers. The INPUT LINK table (disc resident, hashed) maps incoming links to the corresponding connections. Additionally, buffer pages (input and output buffers of 253 words each) are shared between the Network program and user processes for passing messages and control information, and between the Handler and Network program for assembling and disassembling messages word by word.
sections.plainLanguage: The operating system keeps three tables to track which connections are open and which links are available. Special pages in memory let user programs and the network program communicate, and other pages let the hardware interface hand off messages.

sections.title: Handler and Network Programs
sections.content: The Handler is a core-resident I/O interrupt routine that transmits messages to the IMP (Interface Message Processor) and receives messages from it, word by word in full-duplex mode. When transmission or reception completes, the Handler wakes the Network program. The Network program is a regular GORDO process that runs disc-resident but is loaded into core when awakened. It serves users by establishing and closing connections, sending control messages (ENQ, ACK, EOT) to remote hosts to coordinate link establishment, formatting outgoing messages with leaders, marking and checksums, and delivering incoming messages to the appropriate user based on incoming link numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The Hardware Handler reads from and writes to the network connection, one word at a time. The Network program manages the connections, talks to remote computers to set things up, and delivers messages to the right users.

sections.title: Opening Connections and Sending Messages
sections.content: When a user opens a primary connection, it writes a request to the Network mail box, couples a shared page to its virtual space, stores information (job/process number, remote host number), and wakes the Network program, then sleeps. The Network program finds the request, selects a free outgoing link from the HOST table, stores connection information in the CONNECT table, temporarily stores the connection number in the INPUT LINK table, formats a control message (ENQ PRIM with link numbers), checks if the Handler is free, and stores the message for transmission. When the remote host acknowledges with an ACK message, the Network program updates the connection, turns on a bit in the shared page, and wakes the user. Message transmission follows a similar pattern: the user stores data in the shared page's output buffer and wakes the Network program, which picks it up, formats it into a complete message, and gives it to the Handler.
sections.plainLanguage: When a user wants to talk to another computer, it leaves a note and goes to sleep. The network program reads the note, sets up a connection, and wakes the user when it is ready. When the user has data to send, it puts it in a shared memory area and wakes the network program, which sends it out.

references.text: BBN, "Specifications for the Interconnection of a Host and an IMP," Report 1822, January 1976.
